title: A 2008-2016 superorbital model of LS I +61 303 predicts the 2017-2026 Fermi-LAT orbital light-curve shape, but the mean-flux cycle is not stable
abstract: We tested if the 1667-day superorbital cycle of the gamma-ray binary LS I +61 303 is a stable clock at GeV energies. We fitted models to Fermi-LAT Light Curve Repository 3-day fluxes from 2008 to 2016 only, and we predicted 1103 bins from 2017 to 2026-10. We wrote the plan before the test. A quality rule removed 42 bins with failed background fits, most after the 2018 solar-array anomaly. The frozen orbital x superorbital model reduced the weighted squared error by 5.8 percent relative to an orbital-only model. No model of 500 with random superorbital periods reached this value (99th percentile 1.1 percent). The block-bootstrap 95 percent interval was -1.4 to 16.4 percent. The gain came from the superorbital change of the orbital light-curve shape: the sidebands-only model gave 3.8 percent (0.8 to 8.2 percent), and the mean-flux sinusoid gave 1.7 percent (-6.9 to 11.7 percent). The orbital phase of the GeV peak moved with superorbital phase in the same pattern in both decades. The mean-flux cycle decreased to half amplitude, and inside 2017-2026 it preferred a 1417-day period, outside the range of simulations with a 1667-day clock. Six nearby control sources showed no gain. Limitations: the main interval includes zero, the quality rule was added after the first run, the test covers about 2.2 cycles, and we used the fixed LCR analysis without energy resolution. We give a per-orbit forecast for 2026-11 to 2029-12.

display.caption: Orbital phase of the GeV peak, orbital amplitude and mean flux against superorbital phase (1667 d) for 2008-2016 (fit, blue) and 2017-2026 (test, orange). The peak-phase and amplitude patterns repeat; the mean-flux pattern changes.

Left: 2017-2026 skill of frozen 2008-2016 models relative to an orbital-only model, with 95 percent block-bootstrap intervals. Middle: skill for 500 random superorbital periods compared with 1667 d. Right: skill in half-cycle blocks of the test period.

In-sample gain of the orbital x superorbital model against trial superorbital period for 2008-2016, 2017-2026 and all data. The 2017-2026 peak (1417 d) comes from the mean-flux term; the full data peak at 1671 d.
